description_full: Vale S.A., together with its subsidiaries, produces iron ore and nickel in Brazil, Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania. The company operates in two segments, Iron Ore Solutions and Vale Base Metals. It extracts, produces, and distributes iron ore, iron ore pellets, briquettes, nickel, copper, other ferrous products, and by-products, including gold, silver, cobalt, platinum-group metals, and other base metals, as well as low-carbon critical minerals. The company also operates logistics systems and distribution centers, such as mining complexes, railways, and maritime terminals, ports, and ships; generates energy from hydroelectric, solar, and wind sources; and engages in greenfield mineral exploration. In addition, it is involved in research; and trading activities. The company was formerly known as Companhia Vale do Rio Doce and changed its name to Vale S.A. in May 2009. Vale S.A. was founded in 1942 and is headquartered in Rio De Janeiro, Brazil.

financial_summary: VALE S.A. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $49.3B market cap on $48.8B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +27% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are contracting by -2.1pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 8% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $818M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.4% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA.

Management returns a meaningful 7.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.7% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.61).
It converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 3.01x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9 and high accruals (-8.4% of assets).

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($6.1B of cash against $30.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.21 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 26.8% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 46%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 16.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 3.6x depreciation (32.4% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has missed earnings estimates by 28.4% on average.
Analysts expect 8.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 20%.
Insider trading is two-way: 9 purchases and 3 sales over the past year.
It returns 7.2% a year to shareholders (7.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 527% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 65,805 employees, each generates about $741K of revenue, 1.2x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 26.8% a year.
That works out to $12K of free cash flow per employee.
